plain_definition: The process of spreading out a loan into a series of equal regular monthly payments (EMIs) over time that cover both interest and principal.
Pledging an asset (like inventory, machinery, or vehicle) as security for a loan while you continue to keep and use the asset. The lender can seize it only if you default.
A temporary grace period granted by the lender during which you are not required to pay your monthly EMI. Note that interest may still accumulate during this time.
A fee charged by the lender if you pay off the loan before its scheduled tenure ends.
An interest rate linked to an external standard (like Repo Rate or MCLR) that moves up or down whenever central bank interest rates change.
A promise by the borrower that they will not create any debt, mortgage, or claim over their specified assets to any other party without the lender's prior consent.
A fixed payment amount made by a borrower to a lender on a set date each calendar month until the total loan is cleared.
The true yearly cost of borrowing, which includes not just the interest rate but all processing fees, insurance, and administrative charges.
A strict clause that allows the lender to demand immediate full repayment of the entire remaining loan balance if you miss payments or breach terms.
A legally binding promise where an individual (such as a company director or proprietor) pledges their own personal savings, home, and assets if the business cannot repay.
A clause declaring that defaulting on any other separate loan or credit card with any bank automatically puts this loan into default as well.
The legal right of the bank to seize money from your savings, current, or fixed deposit accounts to recover past-due loan balances without needing prior court approval.
An extra punitive interest charge added on top of your standard loan interest rate for late or delayed payments.
Rules and conditions you agree to follow during the loan period, like maintaining minimum bank balances (affirmative) or not taking more debt (negative).
An agreement to compensate the bank for any legal costs, losses, damages, or claims arising from your use of the loan or breach of contract.
A term granting the lender the power to increase interest rates, margins, or spreads at its sole discretion without needing your consent.
Property, cash deposits, or valuable assets pledged to secure a loan, which the lender can take ownership of if the loan is not repaid.
The actual release or transfer of the sanctioned loan funds from the lender to the borrower's bank account.
The total duration or time period agreed upon for repaying the entire loan (e.g., 36 months, 5 years).
A financial metric measuring your business's available cash flow to pay off current debt obligations (interest and principal).
The borrower's own cash contribution towards an asset purchase, or the discount percentage a lender applies when valuing your collateral.
A Latin legal term meaning 'on equal footing'. It ensures multiple lenders sharing the same collateral have equal rights to claim proceeds.
A standardized one-page summary mandated by the RBI detailing the all-inclusive APR, fees, recovery agents, and grievance redressal mechanisms.

term: MCLR (Marginal Cost of Funds Based Lending Rate)
plain_definition: An internal benchmark used by Indian banks to determine minimum interest rates for various loans based on their cost of deposits.
A transparent lending rate directly tied to the RBI's repo rate or government treasury yields, ensuring rapid rate transmission.
A legal claim or restriction on a property or asset, such as a mortgage, lien, or tax liability.
The formal channel or government-appointed authority where borrowers can escalate complaints against unfair lender practices.
A one-time non-refundable charge levied by the bank to evaluate, underwrite, and process your loan application.
Paying off the entire outstanding loan balance in a single lump sum before the end of the loan tenure to close the account.
A mandatory window (typically 3 to 7 days) allowing the borrower to cancel the loan agreement without paying heavy penalties except nominal pro-rata costs.
A formal offer letter from the lender confirming loan approval, sanctioned amount, interest rate, and terms prior to the execution of the full agreement.
An Indian law that allows secured lenders to take possession and auction pledged physical collateral upon default without having to go through prolonged civil court cases.
A specialized third-party bank account holding funds (such as taxes, insurance, or project revenue) that are released only when agreed conditions are met.
How often the lender adjusts your floating interest rate based on changes in the benchmark index (e.g., quarterly or annually).
A government tax paid on loan agreements and mortgage deeds to give them legal evidentiary validity in courts.
A legal clause stating that if any single term of the agreement is found illegal or unenforceable, the remaining contract remains fully valid.
A legal right granted to the lender to hold possession of your property or funds until the debt balance is satisfied.
Modifying loan terms (such as extending tenure or reducing EMI) when a borrower faces severe financial distress.
A clause authorizing the lender to act on your behalf to execute sale documents, transfer collateral, or enforce claims upon default.
A loan where interest or principal installments have remained overdue for 90 days or more.
A fixed initial timeframe during which the borrower is strictly prohibited from prepaying or transferring the loan to another lender.
An agreement ranking this loan below other primary debts so that senior lenders get paid first in a liquidation.
The specific state or city courts whose local laws will settle any legal conflicts arising from the contract.
Fees applied when an automated NACH debit or check for your EMI fails due to insufficient funds.
A revolving credit line sanctioned for day-to-day business operations (payroll, raw materials, inventory).
The percentage of an asset's appraised value that the bank is willing to lend you (e.g. 75% LTV on a ₹1 Crore home means a ₹75 Lakh loan).
The proportion of your gross monthly income that goes towards paying monthly recurring debt obligations.
Interest paid only on the disbursed portion of a home or construction loan before the full property is completed and regular full EMIs begin.
Releasing the loan amount in multiple installments tied to milestones (like building construction progress) rather than all at once.
A mortgage created simply by physically depositing original property title deeds with the lender, without registering a formal sale conveyance deed.
A formal mortgage deed executed and registered at the sub-registrar office, giving public notice of the lender's legal charge on the property.
An official government document showing all registered transactions, claims, and mortgages on a property over a specified historical period.
A signed legal promise by the borrower to repay the entire principal loan amount immediately whenever demanded by the lender.
A security claim over specific, identifiable assets (like a designated factory land or specific machine) that the borrower cannot sell without prior bank approval.
A security claim over fluctuating business assets (like inventory or accounts receivable) that becomes fixed only when a default occurs.
An electronic authorization given to your bank to automatically deduct monthly loan EMIs directly from your account on the scheduled due date.
A credit tracking number that shows exactly how many days have elapsed since a scheduled loan installment due date was missed.
Regulatory classification for early signs of loan stress (SMA-0: 1-30 days overdue, SMA-1: 31-60 days overdue, SMA-2: 61-90 days overdue).
A borrower who has the financial capacity to pay debts but deliberately refuses, or who diverts loan funds for unauthorized purposes.
Specialized quasi-judicial tribunals established in India for rapid recovery of debts due to banks and financial institutions above statutory thresholds.
The Indian law governing time-bound corporate insolvency resolution and liquidation processes before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).
A revolving credit facility allowing businesses to withdraw funds beyond their bank balance up to a sanctioned limit against current assets.
The actual usable portion of a working capital limit calculated monthly based on verified paid stock, inventory, and eligible debtors after deducting margin.
A formal financial document issued by a bank guaranteeing payment to a seller provided specific trade documentation is presented.
A promise by a lending bank to pay a beneficiary if the borrower fails to fulfill performance or financial obligations in a contract.
A disproportionately large lump-sum payment due at the very end of a loan tenure after a period of smaller regular monthly installments.
A repayment structure where the entire principal balance is repaid in a single final lump sum at maturity, with only periodic interest paid in the interim.
A repayment structure where monthly installments start lower in the initial years and gradually increase as the borrower's earnings grow.
A repayment structure where monthly installments start higher and decrease over time, ideal for borrowers nearing retirement.
A negotiated compromise where the lender agrees to accept a discounted lump-sum payment to close a stressed or non-performing loan account.
Expenses incurred by a bank when a borrower repays a fixed-rate loan before maturity, reflecting losses on matching wholesale funding arrangements.
A specialized financial institution that buys bad loans from banks to recover dues or restructure the underlying business.
A periodic verification by an independent chartered accountant of the borrower's pledged inventory and book debts securing working capital loans.
Procedures used by banks (such as CA certificates or direct supplier payments) to ensure loan funds are used strictly for the sanctioned purpose.
An insurance endorsement designating the lending bank as the primary recipient of any insurance payouts if pledged property or machinery is damaged.
A three-digit numeric summary (300 to 900) reflecting a borrower's credit history and repayment reliability based on past loan and card records.
A legal opinion prepared by an advocate investigating property ownership records for 13 to 30 years to verify clear and marketable title.
An assessment by a government-approved valuer determining the fair market value and distress sale value of property or machinery offered as security.
Ancillary fees levied by lenders to draft agreements, inspect collateral, and register security charges on statutory portals like CERSAI.

term: CERSAI (Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest)
plain_definition: The central electronic registry in India where all mortgages and security charges on tangible assets must be registered to prevent duplicate borrowing on the same property.
